title: Parijata Vrittantam
body:
Parijata Vrittantam

The air in Dwaraka was filled with festivity as Krishna and Satyabhama returned triumphant from their battle against Narakasura. The city rejoiced in the Lord's victory, but amid the celebrations a seed of pride began to grow in Satyabhama's heart. Having fought at Krishna's side, she felt herself His most deserving queen, and longed for some grand display of His love.
It was then that the sage Narada arrived in Dwaraka, bearing a single celestial flower — the divine Parijata from the heavenly gardens of Indra's Amaravati. Ever the instigator of divine events, Narada asked Krishna to whom among His queens he should present the flower, and Krishna, smiling, left the choice to the sage. Sensing an opportunity to stir emotions, Narada offered the flower first to Rukmini, Krishna's foremost and most composed queen. Just as it was placed in her hands, Satyabhama happened to walk in, and seeing the divine bloom in Rukmini's hands her heart burned with wounded pride. She turned to Krishna and demanded that, if He truly loved her, He bring her not a single flower but the entire Parijata tree.
Ever aware of His beloved queen's heart, Krishna agreed, and mounting Garuda with Satyabhama, He set out for Amaravati. When He walked toward the Parijata tree to fulfill her wish, Indra objected, declaring that the tree belonged to the gods and was not meant for the mortal world. Satyabhama, unwilling to yield, proclaimed that her Lord was the Supreme Being, and that if He desired the tree, none could stand in His way. Indra summoned his celestial army, and thunder clashed as he charged forth upon Airavata; but Krishna countered the Devas with ease, striking down their weapons and blazing through their ranks with His Sudarshana Chakra, until Indra, realizing the futility of resistance, bowed and conceded defeat, confessing that he had been blinded by pride in forgetting that all worlds belong to the Lord.
Having won, Krishna uprooted the Parijata tree, placed it upon Garuda, and bore it back to Dwaraka, where He planted it in Satyabhama's palace gardens. The tree bloomed gloriously, its fragrance filling the air, and Satyabhama rejoiced, believing she had won Krishna's undivided love. Yet she noticed something peculiar — however the tree was planted, its blossoms always fell at Rukmini's doorstep, and no matter how often she tried, the flowers seemed always to gravitate toward Krishna's first queen. In this she came to see a deeper truth: that divine love cannot be measured in possessions or grand displays, but only in surrender, devotion, and grace. Krishna, ever playful yet ever wise, had fulfilled her desire while teaching her that true love lies not in possession but in trust and humility before the divine will.
